blocks.text: I wanted to gain a friend, not make an enemy. So I thanked him, gave him the address at Dr. Seward’s, and left. It was now dark, and I was tired and hungry. I got a cup of tea at the Aërated Bread Company. Then I took the next train down to Purfleet.

I found all the others at home. Mina looked tired and pale, but she bravely tried to be bright and cheerful. It hurt me deeply to think I had been forced to keep things from her. By doing so, I had made her worried and uneasy. Thank God, this will be the last night she watches us holding our meetings. She will no longer feel hurt because we do not show that we trust her. It took all my courage to keep to our wise decision. We had decided to leave her out of our terrible task. She somehow seems more willing to accept this now. Or perhaps the very subject has become horrible to her. When anyone mentions it by accident, she actually shakes with horror. I am glad we made our decision in time. As she feels this way, the things we are learning would be torture to her.

I could not tell the others what I had discovered that day until we were alone. After dinner, we played a little music to make things seem normal, even to ourselves. Then I took Mina to her room and left her to go to bed. The dear girl showed me more love than ever. She held tightly to me, as though she wanted to keep me there. But there was much to discuss, and I left. Thank God, no longer telling her things has made no difference between us.

When I came down again, the others were all gathered round the fire in the study. On the train, I had written my diary up to that point. I simply read it aloud to them. This was the best way to tell them everything I knew. When I finished, Van Helsing said:

“You have done excellent work today, friend Jonathan. There is no doubt that we are following the trail of the missing boxes. If we find them all in that house, our work is nearly finished. But if some are missing, we must search until we find them. Then we shall strike our final blow. We shall hunt the wretch until he is truly dead.” We all sat in silence for a while. Suddenly Mr. Morris spoke:
“Say! how are we going to get into that house?”
“We got into the other,” answered Lord Godalming quickly.

“But, Art, this is different. We broke into the house at Carfax. But the darkness and the park with its walls protected us. Breaking into a house in Piccadilly will be very different, by day or by night. I admit I cannot see how we will get in unless that fellow at the agency can find us some sort of key. Perhaps we shall know when you get his letter in the morning.” Lord Godalming frowned, stood up, and walked about the room. After a while, he stopped. He turned to each of us in turn and said:

“Quincey is thinking sensibly. This business of breaking into houses is getting serious. We got away with it once, but now we have a very difficult job ahead—unless we can find the Count’s basket of keys.”

There was little we could do before morning. At least, it seemed wise to wait until Lord Godalming heard from Mitchell’s. So we decided to take no action before breakfast time. We sat and smoked for quite a while. We discussed the matter from different sides and considered how everything was connected. I used the chance to bring this diary up to the present moment. I am very sleepy and shall go to bed....

Just a line. Mina is sleeping deeply, and her breathing is steady. There are little lines across her forehead, as though she is thinking even in her sleep. She is still too pale. But she does not look as worn and tired as she did this morning. I hope tomorrow will put all this right. She will be herself again at home in Exeter. Oh, but I am sleepy!
